question: A component renders before setState completes. Why doesn't the state update immediately in: this.setState({ count: 1 }); console.log(this.state.count);?
options: setState is asynchronous and batched, state updates after render
setState is synchronous but logging happens before update
console.log runs in a different execution context
setState fails silently when called in constructor
explanation: setState is asynchronous; React batches updates and re-renders, so this.state.count is still the old value during synchronous code.

question: Why might rendering the same component instance multiple times with different props still show stale props in handlers? function Child({ count }) { return <button onClick={() => console.log(count)}>Click</button>; }
options: The handler closes over the current props, always fresh
Props are captured at function creation time, click logs old value
onClick handlers must use useCallback to see new props
React re-binds handlers on every render automatically
explanation: If Parent doesn't re-render Child, the component function doesn't run again, so the closure captures stale props; re-rendering fixes it.

question: A controlled component updates on every keystroke with onChange. Why might uncontrolled components be faster? <input defaultValue="text" />
options: Uncontrolled skips state update, fewer re-renders of parent
Controlled is actually faster, uncontrolled causes re-renders
Uncontrolled manages its own DOM, avoiding React batching
Both are identical in performance, choice is stylistic
explanation: Uncontrolled input updates the DOM directly without state; no parent re-render needed, reducing work per keystroke.

question: Given a component that uses both state and props, which typically requires more re-renders? function Parent() { const [x, setX] = useState(0); return <Child x={x} z={x} />; }
options: Props cause fewer re-renders because state is internal
State updates cause Parent to re-render, Child always re-renders
Only Child re-renders, Parent state is isolated
State and props are equivalent; re-renders are the same
explanation: State update at Parent triggers Parent re-render, which re-renders Child with new props regardless of whether Child props changed.

question:
Why is a React fragment used instead of a div wrapper? <>{children} vs
{children}
options: Fragment is slightly faster but functionally identical
Fragment doesn't add DOM nodes, avoiding layout thrashing
div is always preferred, fragment is a legacy feature
Fragment preserves CSS grid/flex parent-child relationships
explanation: Fragment doesn't render a DOM element, so it avoids adding an extra node that could break CSS layout (especially grid/flex) or complicate selectors.

question: Why might React.memo(Component) prevent a child from updating even when its props change? const Memoized = React.memo(Child);
options: memo uses shallow equality by default, so nested objects appear unchanged
memo caches props forever, new props are ignored
memo only works with function components, breaks with class
memo prevents all re-renders, defeating prop updates
explanation: React.memo's default equality check compares props with ===; if an object reference didn't change, memo skips re-render even though the object contents changed.

question: Given multiple state setters called in sequence: setState(a); setState(b); setState(c);, how many re-renders occur in React 18+?
options: Three re-renders, one per setter
One re-render, all updates batched into a single commit
Two re-renders, async setters batch with a delay
No re-render until the event handler completes
explanation: React 18 batches all state updates in event handlers and effects, committing once; this reduces re-renders but requires understanding batching boundaries.

question: Why does a key prop matter when rendering a list? Why might list.map(item => <Item key={item.id} />) fail if item.id is not stable?
options: key helps React identify which items changed, deleted, or added
key is optional; React finds items by position automatically
key enforces immutability, preventing accidental mutations
Unstable keys cause re-renders, stable keys skip them
explanation: Unstable keys (like array index or random) trick React into thinking items changed when they didn't, causing state loss and DOM thrashing.

question: A component passes `null` or `undefined` as children: <Parent>{null}</Parent> vs <Parent>{undefined}</Parent>. What renders?
options: Both render nothing, null and undefined are ignored
null renders nothing, undefined throws error
Both render the strings 'null' and 'undefined'
Only undefined is ignored, null renders empty text
explanation: React treats null, undefined, true, and false as empty and renders nothing; this is useful for conditional rendering without empty text nodes.
